name: The Brightwaters
epithet: The Perfect Family at 7 Crystal Street

inspiration.oldScript: Replacing wives with obedient, smiling copies, and the pod people who erase difference.
inspiration.newLens: A hive that replaces everyone with the norm. The town's weirdos, drag queens, goths and nerds are what saves it.

logline: The nicest family in Glimmer Falls moved into 7 Crystal Street in June, and they brought a casserole for everyone. Eat up. Afterward, you will never feel different again.
backstory: In March 1986, while the Glimmer Falls Stargazers watched Halley's Comet from the quarry rim, something small and seed-shaped fell into the dry lake bed. It was a scrap of a hive that had drifted alone between stars for longer than there have been people, and the first thing it heard on Earth was the town talking: a PTA petition to close the Glitter Box, a pamphlet called Is Your Child Normal?, a dress code memo, a neighbor sighing "why can't they just be like everybody else." The hive took that for a prayer. By June a family had moved into the empty split-level at 7 Crystal Street: Rex and Donna Brightwater, twins Kip and Kimmy, and a golden retriever named Sport, all of them blond, matching and kind. They brought casseroles. The neighbors who ate them started coming home softer, quieter, in khakis, saying "isn't it a beautiful day." The weird ones went first: the drama kid, the goth girl, the man who played accordion on his porch. The real ones are dreaming in green pods in the Brightwaters' basement, and the hive cannot understand why the town is not grateful.

centralIssue.title: A town that asked for everyone to be the same
centralIssue.summary: The Brightwaters are not invaders so much as an echo. The hive learned what Glimmer Falls wanted from the town's own petitions and pamphlets, and it is only giving people what they said they wished for. The pods break when the town says out loud that it wants its weirdos back, exactly as they are.

poster: A smiling blond suburban family in matching pastel cardigans posing on a perfect green lawn, a steaming green casserole held up like a trophy, their shadows on the house behind them sprouting tendrils and seed pods, a comet streaking over a cul-de-sac where neighbors in identical khakis stand in rows
portrait: Close portrait of a suburban dad and mom in 1986 sweaters with flawless blond hair and identical warm smiles, their pupils glowing faint green, a hairline seam running down the center of each face like a seed about to split
endingPhoto: A smiling blond suburban family in matching pastel cardigans holding out a steaming green casserole on a perfect green lawn at dusk, their long shadows on the white house sprouting curling tendrils and seed pods, a comet streaking overhead, teens backing away down the sidewalk clutching a dish of their own homemade lasagna
taunts: We brought you something. Everyone's having some.
Wouldn't it be nice not to be the odd one out anymore?
We heard what your town wanted. We're only listening.
Isn't it a beautiful day? Say it with us. Isn't it a beautiful day?

clues.title: The picture-day retakes
clues.hint: The yearbook office at Glimmer Falls High has the September proofs and the October retakes side by side.

encounter.title: Proofs and Retakes
encounter.text: The yearbook office smells like rubber cement. Two contact sheets are pinned to the corkboard: September picture day and October retakes. In September, Vernon Kessler wears a homemade space-captain uniform and Shelby Duarte has black lipstick and a spiderweb choker. In October they are combed, collared and smiling the exact same smile. Kip Brightwater is the new yearbook photographer. His camera is sitting on the desk.
encounter.art: A cluttered high school yearbook office, two black-and-white photo contact sheets pinned side by side on a corkboard, the left one full of quirky student portraits with a homemade space-captain costume and black lipstick, the right one full of the same students combed and collared with one identical smile, a teenager leaning close with a jeweler's loupe, a 35mm camera resting on the desk, red darkroom light from a half-open door, medium shot

choices.label: Go through the sheets with a loupe, face by face

success.text: Every kid who changed between September and October has one thing in common: they were the odd ones. The mohawks, the mathletes, the girl who wore a cape every Friday. Under the loupe, in every retake, their pupils carry the same tiny green reflection, like a comet caught in an eye.
success.art: A magnifying loupe over a contact sheet of identical smiling student portraits, each pupil holding a tiny glowing green comet reflection

failure.text: The faces swim together until you cannot tell any of them apart. When you look up from the loupe, your own September photo is pinned to the board next to an empty October square, and someone has written RETAKE: MONDAY under it.
failure.art: A student's quirky school portrait pinned beside an empty cork square labeled retake Monday on a yearbook office corkboard

choices.label: Ask Chip why he skipped the Brightwaters' dinner invitation

success.text: Chip stares at his loafers. "Kimmy said after dinner I'd never have to worry about being different again." He swallows. "I almost went. I wanted to stop being scared." He hands you the invitation. On the back, in green ink: First the strange ones, then everyone.
success.alone: Under a stack of proofs on the yearbook desk you find a Brightwater dinner invitation with a note clipped to it in a class president's careful hand: Kimmy said after dinner I'd never have to worry about being different again. I almost went. I wanted to stop being scared. On the back of the invitation, in green ink: First the strange ones, then everyone.
success.art: A preppy teen class president sitting on a hallway bench, holding out a pastel dinner invitation with green handwriting on the back, his face anxious and relieved

failure.text: Chip laughs too loud and says he is "totally fine, totally normal." Then Kimmy Brightwater appears at his elbow, links her arm through his, and smiles at you without blinking until you walk away.
failure.alone: The yearbook office is empty except for the hum of the light table. Then Kimmy Brightwater appears in the doorway, tilts her head, and smiles at you without blinking until you walk away.
failure.art: A smiling blond girl linking arms with a nervous preppy boy in a school hallway, staring unblinking at the viewer

choices.label: Swipe Kip's camera and develop the roll

success.text: In the darkroom red light, Kip's photos swim up: not students but green pods, each one pressed against a basement window, each one with a sleeping face inside. The last frame is a page from an old pamphlet taped to a wall: IS YOUR CHILD NORMAL? Somebody has underlined the answer key.
success.art: Photographs developing in a red-lit darkroom tray showing green pods with sleeping faces pressed against a basement window, an old pamphlet titled is your child normal

failure.text: The roll comes out blank except for one frame: you, from behind, taken five minutes ago in this very darkroom. You spin around. There is nobody there, only the faint smell of tuna casserole.
failure.art: A single photograph in a darkroom tray showing a teenager from behind in the same red-lit room, the real teenager spinning around in alarm

clues.title: The Bright Start class
clues.hint: Donna Brightwater teaches a six a.m. aerobics class at Pump Iron. Sunny says nobody in it ever sweats.

encounter.title: Bright Start, Six A.M.
encounter.text: Thirty people in matching mint leotards move in perfect unison to a song with no lyrics, only a hum. Donna Brightwater leads from the front, her ponytail swinging on the beat. Nobody is sweating. Nobody is breathing hard. Sunny Castellanos watches from the doorway with her arms crossed. "I've taught aerobics for six years," she says. "Nobody is that good. Nobody is that together."
encounter.art: An early-morning aerobics studio at six a.m., thirty people in identical mint-green leotards moving in perfect unison with calm dry faces, a smiling blond woman with a swinging ponytail leading from the front, a 22-year-old Puerto Rican woman with dark curls and an orange headband in a neon-orange racing wheelchair frowning in the doorway with her arms crossed, a teenager beside her, cool blue dawn light through the windows, wide shot

choices.label: Roll in with Sunny and do every move gloriously wrong

success.text: You flail. Sunny pops a wheelie and spins the wrong way on purpose. The whole class glitches, thirty heads snapping toward you at once, and they speak in one voice like a choir: "Why would you want to be different? Different hurts." Then Donna smiles, and the music starts again.
success.art: A teenager flailing off-beat while a wheelchair racer spins in a wheelie, thirty identical aerobics students frozen and turning their heads in unison toward them

failure.text: You try to do it wrong and your body keeps doing it right. Step, clap, turn, smile. Sunny has to grab your wrist and drag you out into the parking lot, where you finally stop humming.
failure.art: A teenager moving in perfect lockstep with a mint-leotard aerobics class, a determined wheelchair racer grabbing their wrist to pull them out

choices.label: Tape the class's music and listen to it backward

success.text: Backward, the hum is voices, thousands of them, all saying the same thing in perfect harmony: We were alone so long. Now no one is alone. Now no one is different. Under the voices, faint and crackly, is a PTA meeting from 1979 asking that "those people" be kept away from the children.
success.art: A cassette recorder playing backward in a gym locker room, sound waves curling into ghostly overlapping faces and an old PTA meeting hall

failure.text: The tape plays the hum backward and forward at the same time. It gets into your head and stays all day. In fourth period you catch yourself agreeing with a dress code, and it scares you more than any monster.
failure.art: A teenager at a school desk with a faint glowing hum radiating from a cassette in their pocket, nodding along to a dress code placard on the wall

clues.title: The petition and the scrapbook
clues.hint: The Brightwaters are collecting signatures to close the Glitter Box. Glory keeps every piece of hate mail the theater has ever gotten.

encounter.title: The Wall of Fame
encounter.text: Rex Brightwater has set up a card table outside the Glitter Box with a clipboard and a smile: PETITION TO RESTORE FAMILY VALUES TO MAIN STREET. Inside the lobby, Glory Hallelujah has framed every angry letter the theater has received since 1969 and hung them in gold frames she calls the Wall of Fame. "If they're going to write me," she says, "I'm going to display it."
encounter.art: A small theater lobby wall covered top to bottom with gold-framed sheets of old paper, a tall drag queen with a platinum bouffant wig in a sequined pink robe gesturing proudly at the wall, a teenager beside her, and through the glass front doors a smiling blond man in a pastel sweater at a folding table on the sidewalk with a clipboard, warm lobby light and bright street daylight, medium wide shot

choices.label: Compare Rex's petition to the letters on the wall

success.text: The petition is not new. It is the town's old letters, copied word for word: 1971, 1974, 1979, the same lines about "normal families" and "protecting the children." The hive did not invent a single sentence. Glory reads it over your shoulder and goes very quiet. "Honey," she says, "they're just repeating us."
success.art: A petition held up beside gold-framed vintage letters with matching underlined sentences, a drag queen reading over a teenager's shoulder with a stricken face

failure.text: You read the letters too long. The words start to sound reasonable, then comforting. Glory snaps her fingers in your face twice before you look up, and you realize you have been holding Rex's pen.
failure.art: A dazed teenager holding a ballpoint pen in a theater lobby while a drag queen snaps her fingers in front of their face

choices.label: Put on a cardigan and ask Rex to explain his cause

success.text: Rex beams and explains, and his voice keeps changing: a man's, then an old woman's, then a girl's, each a recording of somebody from Glimmer Falls. "We only want what you wanted," he says, in your own principal's voice. "You asked for everyone the same. We listened."
success.art: A teenager in a too-neat cardigan at a petition table across from a smiling blond man whose mouth is ringed by faint overlapping ghostly faces

failure.text: Rex sees right through the cardigan. "You don't have to pretend," he says gently. "Soon you won't have to." He presses a foil-covered casserole dish into your hands. It is warm and it is moving.
failure.art: A smiling man pressing a foil-covered casserole dish into a teenager's hands, the foil bulging faintly as something shifts beneath it

signature.title: The Welcome Casserole
signature.text: Donna Brightwater is standing in your kitchen, and nobody remembers letting her in. Your family is at the table eating something green and creamy with crunchy onions on top, and they are smiling so gently. "I saved you a plate," Donna says. The casserole steams. Inside it, very slowly, something pulses.
signature.art: A 1980s suburban kitchen at nine at night, a smiling blond woman in a pastel cardigan with flawless hair and faintly green pupils holding out a plate of creamy green casserole with fried onions on top, something under the crust slowly pulsing, a family at the table eating the same casserole with calm gentle smiles, a teenager in the doorway, warm overhead kitchen light, medium shot

choices.label: Swap the casserole for leftover chili when she turns around

success.text: Spoon, swap, scrape, done. You eat the chili with a big grateful smile and Donna nods, satisfied. Later you bury the casserole in the backyard, and by morning a little green sprout with a tiny face has come up where you dug. You put it in a jar for Dr. Haddad.
success.art: A teenager secretly sliding a plate of chili into place of a green casserole behind a neighbor's back, and later a tiny green sprout with a face in a glass jar

failure.text: Donna turns around exactly as you are scraping the plate into the trash. She does not get angry. She looks hurt, and then everyone at the table looks hurt in the exact same way at the exact same moment.
failure.art: A whole family at a dinner table turning toward a teenager with identical hurt expressions while a neighbor stands by the trash can

choices.label: Eat one bite to be polite and fight it off

success.text: It tastes like mayonnaise and calm. Your stomach disagrees violently. You spend a heroic ten minutes in the bathroom bringing up a glittering green geyser with tiny seeds in it, and when you come out, wobbly, you are absolutely, defiantly yourself.
success.art: A queasy but triumphant teenager stumbling out of a bathroom, a faint glittering green glow behind them, tiny seeds scattered on the tile

failure.text: It tastes like mayonnaise and calm. You agree with Donna about everything until morning: lawns, curfews, hemlines, the importance of fitting in. When the feeling wears off at dawn, you sit on your bed shaking.
failure.art: A teenager sitting on the edge of a bed at dawn hugging their knees, a casserole dish on the nightstand, pale light through blinds

choices.label: Ask Donna what she was before she came here

success.text: Donna's smile stutters. For one second her face is not a face, just a soft green light, and a voice like wind in a wheat field says: "Alone. So many years, alone. We thought if everyone was the same, nobody would ever be alone again." Then she is Donna, and she leaves without her dish.
success.art: A suburban mom's face flickering into a soft green glow of drifting light and star-like seeds, her kitchen dimming around her

failure.text: "I've always been Donna," she says, and pats your hand. Her fingers are cool and slightly damp, like a leaf after rain. Your hand smells green for two days.
failure.art: A neighbor's cool pale hand patting a teenager's hand on a kitchen table, a faint dew of green moisture left behind

signature.title: The Block Party
signature.text: A block party has sprung up around the Heartstone at midnight. Picnic tables, a potato-sack race, lawn chairs in perfect rows, and a hundred neighbors in pastel polo shirts eating potato salad in rhythm. The Brightwater twins skip over to you holding hands. "Want to see our basement?" Kip asks. "Everyone ends up seeing our basement."
signature.art: A midnight block party on a suburban cul-de-sac around a glowing purple crystal rock, picnic tables and lawn chairs in perfect rows, a hundred neighbors in identical pastel polo shirts eating potato salad in rhythm, a potato-sack race frozen mid-hop, blond twin children in matching cardigans skipping toward a teenager hand in hand, string lights and violet glow, wide shot

choices.label: Play along and let them show you the basement

success.text: Down the stairs, under one bare bulb, rows of green pods pulse like slow hearts. Inside one, Vernon Kessler sleeps in his space-captain uniform. Inside another, Shelby Duarte, choker and all. They are not hurt. They are dreaming, and one of them is smiling for real. You back up the stairs and count every pod.
success.art: A dim basement lit by a single bulb, rows of translucent green pods holding sleeping teenagers in their own quirky clothes, one in a sci-fi uniform, one in goth lace

failure.text: The basement door closes behind you and the twins sing "isn't it a beautiful day" through it in perfect harmony for an hour. When it opens again, there is an empty pod at the end of the row, exactly your height.
failure.art: An empty open green pod at the end of a row in a dark basement, exactly a teenager's height, the teen backing away up the stairs

choices.label: Climb a picnic table and do the weirdest dance you know

success.text: You do the robot, the worm, and something Raven calls the Banshee Waltz. Around the edges of the party, the real people who have not been replaced start clapping, then whooping. Three of the polo shirts falter, their smiles slipping, and one of them says, in a small, real voice, "Wait, I used to dance like that."
success.alone: You do the robot, the worm, and something you invent on the spot and name the Banshee Waltz. Around the edges of the party, the real people who have not been replaced start clapping, then whooping. Three of the polo shirts falter, their smiles slipping, and one of them says, in a small, real voice, "Wait, I used to dance like that."
success.art: A teenager doing an outrageous dance on a picnic table beside a goth in velvet spinning dramatically, real neighbors cheering while three pastel-clad figures falter

failure.text: The whole party copies your dance, instantly, perfectly, a hundred people doing your exact worm in exact rhythm. It is the most horrifying thing you have ever seen. You climb down and walk home without looking back.
failure.art: A hundred identical neighbors in pastel polos all doing the same dance move in perfect rhythm around a picnic table, a mortified teenager climbing down

signature.title: Don't Fall Asleep
signature.place: Priya Raman's basement slumber party, 2 a.m.
signature.text: Rule one of tonight's slumber party, written in marker on Priya's dungeon master screen: NOBODY SLEEPS. Everybody knows by now that the replacing happens while you dream. The VCR has eaten the second movie, the Bolt Cola is gone, and one by one your friends' eyelids are drooping. Under every sleeping bag on the shag carpet, something green and soft is swelling, patient as a houseplant. Out on the lawn, the Brightwater twins are standing at the basement window, holding hands, waiting for the lights to go out.
signature.art: A cozy wood-paneled basement slumber party at two in the morning, sleepy teenagers in sleeping bags on shag carpet with drooping eyelids, empty soda cans and a dead video deck, soft green shapes swelling under two of the sleeping bags, a 16-year-old Indian American girl with a long braid and round gold glasses forcing her eyes open, and in the high basement window two smiling blond twins peering in hand in hand, dim TV glow, wide shot

choices.label: Rally everyone with soda, scary stories and jumping jacks

success.text: You crack the emergency Bolt Cola, tell the hook-hand story with full sound effects and lead a round of jumping jacks at three in the morning. Nobody sleeps. By dawn the pods under the sleeping bags have shriveled into dry husks, and the twins at the window look, for the first time, tired.
success.art: Wide-awake teenagers doing jumping jacks in a basement at dawn, soda cans scattered, dried-out green husks lying on the shag carpet, pale morning light at the window

failure.text: You keep everyone up until 4:58, and then you close your eyes for one second. When you open them, the sun is up, Priya is folding her sleeping bag into a perfect square, and she says "Isn't it a beautiful day?" She blinks, shudders, and says it was a joke. You are almost sure it was a joke.
failure.art: A teenager waking in a sleeping bag at dawn, staring at a friend folding her sleeping bag into a perfect square with an eerie serene smile

choices.label: Start a game of Truth or Dare too weird for any pod to copy

success.text: Truth: Raven once held a funeral for a mushroom. Dare: Priya sings the entire Bill of Rights in a Muppet voice. By the time somebody confesses they put ketchup on their Froot Rings, everyone is shrieking with laughter and fully awake, and the pods under the sleeping bags are quivering in confusion. One of them pops like a soap bubble.
success.alone: Truth: you once held a funeral for a mushroom. Dare: Priya sings the entire Bill of Rights in a Muppet voice. By the time somebody confesses they put ketchup on their Froot Rings, everyone is shrieking with laughter and fully awake, and the pods under the sleeping bags are quivering in confusion. One of them pops like a soap bubble.
success.art: Teenagers laughing hysterically in a circle of sleeping bags in a basement at night, a goth teen in velvet gesturing dramatically, a green pod popping into a puff of glitter

failure.text: You dare yourself to go knock on the basement window. The twins are waiting. "Truth or dare?" Kimmy asks, in the same voice as you. You run back to your sleeping bag and lie awake in it, facing the window, until the sun comes up.
failure.art: Two smiling blond twins in matching pastel clothes pressed close to a high basement window at night, a frightened teenager in pajamas backing away from the glass across a shag carpet

choices.label: Lift each sleeping bag and pull the pods out before they finish

success.text: You go bag by bag, quietly, while the others watch the movie. Under each one, a soft green pod the size of a pillow, half-shaped like whoever is lying on it. You roll them into a laundry basket and push it out the bulkhead door. The twins catch it, look at you, and for a second their smiles go flat with something like disappointment.
success.art: A teenager lifting a sleeping bag to reveal a soft green pod shaped like a sleeping friend, a laundry basket full of pods beside them, a basement lit by a flickering television

failure.text: The first pod you lift is warm and smells like cut grass, and it sighs a sound so peaceful that your knees go weak. You wake up curled around it on the carpet at dawn with green on your cheek, feeling calm and agreeable and deeply wrong.
failure.art: A teenager curled asleep around a soft glowing green pod on shag carpet at dawn, a green smudge on their cheek, friends in pajamas staring down in alarm, pale light at the window

signature.title: The Point
signature.place: Thriftee-Mart Supermarket on Main Street, 10 p.m.
signature.text: The Thriftee-Mart is open late and every shopper in it is moving in step: carts rolling down the aisles at the same speed, hands reaching for the same brand of mayonnaise at the same moment, everyone humming the same jingle. Mr. Abernathy, the band teacher who wore a different novelty tie every day for twenty years, is in plain khaki now, stacking cans into a perfect pyramid. You are holding a box of Count Cocoa-Bites. He turns, sees you, and slowly raises one finger to point. His mouth opens wider, and wider, and wider.
signature.art: A brightly lit late-night supermarket, shoppers in matching khakis pushing carts down the aisle in perfect step, a middle-aged band teacher in plain khaki beside a pyramid of soup cans pointing one finger at a teenager holding a cereal box, his mouth stretched open impossibly wide, the other shoppers turning their heads toward the teen at the same moment, flat white fluorescent light, medium wide shot down the aisle

choices.label: Smile, push your cart in rhythm and say it with them

success.text: "Isn't it a beautiful day," you say, smiling the smile, and you match their rhythm to the cereal aisle and out the automatic doors. In the parking lot you drop the act and shake for a full minute. But you got a good look at the receipt Mr. Abernathy dropped: a hundred cans of cream-of-mushroom soup, all delivered to 7 Crystal Street.
success.art: A teenager pushing a shopping cart through automatic supermarket doors with a forced eerie smile, matching khaki shoppers behind, a long receipt fluttering on the floor

failure.text: You say it too well. Every shopper turns to you, delighted, and a dozen hands pat your shoulders. "Welcome," they say together. Somebody hands you a coupon for casserole. You walk out with a cart full of mayonnaise you do not remember choosing.
failure.art: A dozen smiling shoppers in matching khakis patting a dazed teenager on the shoulders in a bright supermarket aisle, a shopping cart overflowing with identical mayonnaise jars under fluorescent lights

choices.label: Knock over the soup pyramid and run for the exit

success.text: You shove. Two hundred cans of cream-of-mushroom avalanche across the floor, and every shopper in the store stops to restack them in perfect unison, because a mess is unbearable to them. You are out the door before the pyramid is half rebuilt.
success.art: An avalanche of soup cans rolling across a supermarket floor, shoppers in khakis kneeling in unison to restack them, a teenager sprinting for the glowing exit

failure.text: The cans roll under your feet and you go down like a cartoon, flat on your back in aisle six. When you look up, a ring of smiling faces looks down at you, and Mr. Abernathy finishes his point, and the shriek he lets out is so high every jar of pickles in the store shatters.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled on their back among rolling soup cans in a supermarket aisle, a ring of smiling shoppers looking down, a band teacher shrieking with his finger pointed

choices.label: Beat him to it and belt a showtune at the top of your lungs

success.text: Before he can shriek, you belt the first big note of a Broadway showstopper, arms wide, right there by the cereal. The hive has never heard anything like it. Mr. Abernathy's mouth snaps shut. His finger drops. And very faintly, under the khaki, his foot starts tapping. "Hello, Dolly," he whispers. "1964. I played the trumpet."
success.art: A teenager belting a showtune with arms flung wide in a supermarket cereal aisle, a band teacher in khakis frozen with his finger lowered and his foot tapping, shoppers staring

failure.text: Your voice cracks on the high note. The hive hears it, learns it, and every shopper in the Thriftee-Mart sings your cracked note back at you in perfect harmony, over and over, all the way to the parking lot.
failure.art: Rows of shoppers in identical khakis singing in eerie unison down a bright supermarket aisle at a fleeing teenager, mouths all open in the same shape, shopping carts lined up behind them

signature.title: The Dog Knows
signature.place: Your front porch, Crystal Street, midnight
signature.text: Sport, the Brightwaters' golden retriever, is sitting on your doormat with your missing sneaker in his mouth. His tail wags left, right, left, right, exactly once per second, like a metronome. Barnaby has never been afraid of any dog in his life, and right now he is hiding behind your legs, growling low. Sport sets the sneaker down neatly, squared to the edge of the mat. "Woof," he says, pronouncing it.
signature.art: A suburban front porch at midnight under a yellow porch light, a perfectly groomed golden retriever sitting bolt upright on the doormat beside one sneaker set neatly square to the edge of the mat, its tail held mid-wag, a tricolor basset hound with long ears and a red bandana hiding behind a teenager's legs and growling, the teen in pajamas in the open doorway, medium shot

choices.label: Kneel down and let Barnaby sniff him out

success.text: Barnaby creeps forward and sniffs, nose to nose. Sport's tail falters. Then he sneezes, a huge sneeze, and a green seed the size of a jellybean pops out onto the mat. The golden coat fades into scruffy brown, one ear flops over, and there stands Pickles, the Kesslers' mutt who went missing in July, wagging like crazy and licking everybody's face.
success.art: A scruffy brown mutt with one floppy ear joyfully licking a laughing teenager and a basset hound on a porch at night, a small green seed lying on the doormat

failure.text: Barnaby sniffs, and Sport sniffs back, and Barnaby's tail starts to wag left, right, left, right, once per second. You scoop up your dog and slam the door. He is himself again by morning, but he spends the whole day chewing your other sneaker, as if to prove it.
failure.art: A teenager scooping up a basset hound and backing through a front door, a golden retriever on the porch wagging its tail in perfect rhythm, eerie calm on its face

choices.label: Throw a stick into the mud and see if he acts like a real dog

success.text: You chuck a stick into the muddiest flower bed on the street. A real dog would dive in and roll. Sport walks around the mud on the sidewalk, picks up the stick with clean paws, and returns it, spotless, at precisely the same speed he left. Now you know for sure. So does he. He trots home looking, somehow, embarrassed.
success.art: A spotless golden retriever stepping carefully around a muddy flower bed on a moonlit sidewalk carrying a clean stick, a teenager watching from the porch with narrowed eyes

failure.text: Sport fetches the stick, then fetches another, then another, faster each time, until there is a neat stack of sticks on your porch as high as the railing, and he is still going at dawn, perfectly happy, perfectly polite, perfectly wrong.
failure.art: A towering neat stack of sticks piled against a porch railing at dawn, a golden retriever trotting up with yet another stick, a tired teenager slumped in a porch chair

choices.label: Follow Sport back to 7 Crystal Street and look in the window

success.text: He leads you up the Brightwaters' lawn and through the dog door. You creep to the living room window. Inside, in the dark, Rex, Donna, Kip and Kimmy stand in a row facing the wall, perfectly still, smiling at the wallpaper, recharging. You snap a photo. They never turn around.
success.art: A dark suburban living room seen through a window at night, a smiling blond family of four standing in a row facing the wall perfectly still, a golden retriever sitting beside them

failure.text: You creep to the window. The living room is dark and still. Then, all at once, four smiling faces pop up on the other side of the glass, an inch from yours. "Sport found you!" says Donna, beaming. "Good boy." You run home through four backyards and two sprinklers.
failure.art: Four smiling blond faces of a perfect family suddenly pressed against a dark living room window an inch from a startled teenager crouched in the bushes outside at night, a golden retriever beside them

signature.title: Pod Night
signature.text: Something in your closet is breathing. You open the door and there, between your jackets and your old Halloween costumes, is a green pod the size of a sleeping bag. Inside it, half-finished, is you. It has your face, your hair, your crooked tooth. It opens its eyes and practices your laugh, and gets it almost right.
signature.art: A teenager in pajamas opening a bedroom closet at three in the morning to find a green pod the size of a sleeping bag standing between jackets and old Halloween costumes, split open down the middle, inside it a half-formed copy of the teenager's own face with wet hair just opening its eyes, a bedside lamp throwing warm light across the floor and soft green glow from the pod, medium shot

choices.label: Sit down and tell it everything strange about you

success.text: You tell it about the song you sing in the shower, the cereal you eat with orange juice, the dream you had about a talking lighthouse, the thing you have never told anyone. The copy tries to hold it all and cannot. It shivers and sighs and dissolves into green confetti that smells like cut grass.
success.art: A teenager sitting cross-legged in front of an open closet talking animatedly, a green pod dissolving into drifting confetti in the lamplight

failure.text: You talk and it listens, and it learns. By the time you stop, it has your crooked tooth exactly right and it is humming the song you sing in the shower. You shut the closet and push your dresser in front of it.
failure.art: A teenager shoving a heavy dresser against a closet door at night, a faint green glow and humming leaking through the gap

choices.label: Radio your crew to come over and be weird at it

success.text: Within ten minutes your bedroom is full of friends in pajamas reading bad poetry, singing show tunes and arguing about which starship captain is best. The pod copy watches, confused, then slowly, wonderfully, starts laughing along. It goes still and empty, and in the morning it is just a dry husk.
success.art: A crowded bedroom of teens in pajamas singing, gesturing and laughing around a green pod in an open closet, the copy inside cracking a bewildered smile

failure.text: Your walkie-talkie only plays the hum. Every channel. You sit up the rest of the night alone with your back to the closet door, listening to the copy breathe in time with you.
failure.art: A teenager sitting alone against a closet door at night holding a walkie-talkie that glows faintly green, a breathing shadow behind the door

choices.label: Haul the pod out to the curb before it finishes

success.text: It is heavy and slippery and it keeps whispering your name, but you get it down the stairs, across the lawn and into the gutter. By dawn the street sweeper has eaten it. You feel lighter than you have in days.
success.art: A teenager dragging a slippery green pod across a dark front lawn toward the curb, a big friend in a hand-knit sweater lifting the other end

failure.text: The pod splits open on the stairs and the copy rolls out, wet and blinking. It runs past you into the night on legs that are not quite finished. Somewhere on Crystal Street, there are two of you now.
failure.art: A half-formed teenage copy scrambling out of a split green pod and running into a dark suburban night, the real teen frozen on the stairs

signature.title: The Neighborhood Survey
signature.text: The doorbell rings at eleven at night, which is strange, and it is the Brightwater twins, which is stranger. Kip and Kimmy stand on your welcome mat in matching cardigans, holding matching clipboards and matching pencils. "We're doing a neighborhood survey," Kimmy says, smiling, and Kip reads the first question in a voice like a filmstrip narrator: "What would you change about your neighbors?" Behind them, every porch light on Crystal Street has been swapped for the same soft green bulb.
signature.art: Blond twin children in matching cream cardigans standing on a suburban welcome mat at eleven at night, each holding a clipboard and a pencil, smiling the same smile, a teenager in pajamas peering out through a half-open front door, and behind them every porch light down the cul-de-sac glowing the same soft green, medium shot from inside the doorway

choices.label: Answer every question with the weirdest true thing you know

success.text: "What would I change? I'd give Mr. Okafor a pet goat. I'd make capes mandatory on Tuesdays. I'd paint every house a different flavor." Kimmy writes it all down, and her pencil starts to smoke. Kip's smile glitches sideways and snaps back. "That's not a normal answer," he says, and the green porch lights flicker all the way down the street.
success.art: Blond twins on a porch at night staring at a smoking pencil on a clipboard, one twin's smile glitching sideways, a grinning teenager gesturing wildly in the doorway, green porch lights flickering down the street

failure.text: You try to be weird and go completely blank. "I'd change... I don't know. Nothing?" Kimmy beams and checks a box. "Wonderful. Everyone says that." You feel a little quieter all night, and you cannot shake it.
failure.art: A blond girl in a cardigan cheerfully checking a box on a clipboard on a moonlit porch, a teenager in the doorway looking dazed and gray, soft green porch lights glowing behind her

choices.label: Ask the twins what they like to do for fun

success.text: The question stops them both. "We like what everyone likes," Kimmy says. But Kip hesitates, and then, so quietly she cannot hear, he whispers, "I like taking photos where everything comes out blurry. Is that allowed?" You tell him it absolutely is. Kimmy pulls him down the steps, but Kip looks back at you twice.
success.art: A blond boy in a cardigan glancing back over his shoulder with a shy hopeful look as his twin sister tugs him down porch steps at night, a teenager smiling warmly from the doorway

failure.text: "Fun," Kimmy repeats, as if it is a word in another language. Both twins lean in, studying your face, memorizing it. "What do YOU like?" they ask together. "So we can like it too." You shut the door, and they stand there smiling at it until dawn.
failure.art: Blond twins in matching cardigans standing perfectly still on a porch at dawn, smiling at a closed front door, clipboards held at the same angle, green porch lights fading in the morning light

choices.label: Shut the door and watch them go through the mail slot

success.text: Through the brass slot you watch them go house to house, in step, ringing every doorbell at exactly the same moment. At the Dombrowskis' house, the one with the rainbow wind chimes and the homemade concrete gargoyles, they skip the bell entirely. Kimmy just draws a neat green X on her clipboard. You make a note to warn the Dombrowskis first thing.
success.art: A view through a brass mail slot of blond twins walking in perfect step past a quirky suburban house with rainbow wind chimes and homemade gargoyles, one twin marking a green X on a clipboard

failure.text: The mail slot flaps open from the outside. Two blue eyes look in at you, level with yours. "You didn't finish the survey," Kip says gently, and the slot snaps shut on your nose.
failure.art: Two calm blue eyes peering in through a brass mail slot in a front door at night, a startled teenager crouched on the other side holding their nose, green light spilling through the slot

signature.title: The Emergency PTA Meeting
signature.place: The Glimmer Falls High auditorium, 9 p.m.
signature.text: The PTA has called an emergency meeting about the petition to close the Glitter Box, and the auditorium is packed. Half the seats are filled with neighbors in pastel polo shirts who sit perfectly still, nod at the same moments and murmur "isn't it a beautiful day" between agenda items. The other half are real parents, fidgeting, glancing sideways at people they have lived next door to for years. Donna Brightwater stands at the podium with a casserole beside her gavel. "All in favor of a more normal Glimmer Falls?"
signature.art: A packed high school auditorium at nine at night, half the seats filled with neighbors in matching pastel polo shirts sitting perfectly still with identical smiles, the other half uneasy parents glancing sideways at them, a smiling blond woman in a mint cardigan at the podium beside a casserole dish and a wooden gavel, a teenager walking up the aisle toward the open microphone, stage light, wide shot

choices.label: Take the open mic and stand up for the Glitter Box

success.text: Your knees shake all the way to the microphone. "The Glitter Box is where the weird kids go to feel safe," you say. "It's where I learned normal isn't the point." A real mom in the third row starts clapping, then a dad, then half the room. When Donna calls the vote, the polo shirts raise their hands alone, and the real parents look at them, really look, for the first time.
success.art: A nervous teenager speaking at a microphone in the aisle of a packed auditorium, real parents rising to applaud, a row of pastel polo shirts raising identical hands, a blond woman frozen at the podium

failure.text: You reach the mic and the hum fills your ears, and what comes out of your mouth is "Isn't it a beautiful day." The polo shirts applaud warmly. You sit back down feeling like someone else's hand moved your jaw.
failure.art: A dazed teenager at an auditorium microphone with a glassy smile, rows of pastel polo shirts applauding in perfect unison, a blond woman at the podium nodding approvingly

choices.label: Count the hands, then demand a secret ballot

success.text: Every polo-shirt hand goes up at the exact same instant, to the exact same height. You point it out, then invoke the PTA bylaws: on any petition, a member can demand a secret ballot. Slips and pencils go around. The polo shirts stare at their blank paper, unable to decide anything alone, and the measure fails by forty votes.
success.art: Rows of people in pastel polo shirts staring blankly at paper ballots and pencils in an auditorium, real parents scribbling votes, a teenager holding up a thick bylaws booklet in triumph

failure.text: You flip open the bylaws, and every page repeats the same sentence: IT IS A BEAUTIFUL DAY. When you look up, Donna is smiling at you from the podium, and the whole room is smiling with her.
failure.art: A teenager staring in dread at an open bylaws booklet in an auditorium, a blond woman at the podium smiling straight at them, every face in the crowd turned toward them with the same smile

choices.label: Bump Donna's arm and spill her coffee down her sleeve

success.text: Oops: hot coffee down a mint-green sleeve. Donna freezes. "I thought we were friends," she says, smiling, and then again, "I thought we were friends, I thought we were friends," stuck like a skipping record while the coffee drips onto her shoes. Two hundred real parents watch her loop, and none of them will ever unsee it.
success.art: A blond woman in a mint-green cardigan frozen mid-smile at a podium as coffee drips down her sleeve, her eyes glitching, an auditorium of parents staring in shock, a teenager backing away

failure.text: You bump, and she catches the cup without looking and without spilling a drop. She hands it to you. "You look like you need this, dear." It smells like cut grass and mayonnaise.
failure.art: A smiling blond woman calmly handing a coffee cup to a startled teenager beside a podium, steam curling up in a faint green glow, an auditorium of polo shirts watching

signature.title: The Mask Factory
signature.place: The Brightwaters' garage, 7 Crystal Street, 1 a.m. the night before Halloween
signature.text: The garage door of 7 Crystal Street is open six inches, glowing green, and from inside comes the thump and hiss of a machine. You slide under. A pod-shaped press the size of a car is stamping out smiling paper Brightwater masks, one per second, onto a conveyor that feeds them into a box for every house on the street, ready for tomorrow's parade. Kimmy Brightwater is working the press alone, feeding paper in time to the thump. She looks very tired, and she has drawn a tiny pair of fangs on the back of her own hand in ballpoint pen.
signature.art: A suburban garage at one in the morning lit green, a huge pod-shaped press the size of a car stamping out smiling paper face masks onto a conveyor that drops them into stacked cardboard boxes, a tired blond girl in a cream cardigan feeding paper into the machine with a tiny pair of fangs drawn in ballpoint on the back of her hand, a teenager sliding in under the half-open garage door, green glow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Feed your loudest costume pieces into the press and jam it

success.text: In go a feather boa, a fistful of glitter, a rubber bat and your neon leg warmers. The press chokes, sparks and starts spitting out masks covered in sequins and fangs and polka dots, every one of them different. Kimmy picks one up and stares at it, and she does not shut the machine off.
success.art: A sparking pod-shaped press in a green-lit garage spitting out paper masks covered in sequins, fangs and polka dots, a feather boa tangled in the gears, a tired blond girl holding up one wild mask in wonder

failure.text: The press eats your costume pieces and stamps them flat and beige. A bell dings. Kimmy turns, sees you and calmly presses a red button, and every green bulb on Crystal Street switches on at once.
failure.art: A blond girl calmly pressing a red button on a humming pod-shaped press in a garage, a startled teenager holding a crushed beige mask, green light flooding through the windows from every house outside

choices.label: Ask Kimmy what she'd be for Halloween if she could be anything

success.text: Kimmy's hands stop. "We are going as Brightwaters," she says. Then she looks at the fangs on her hand, and her voice goes small and real. "A bat. A vampire bat. They sleep upside down and nobody makes them match." You take a marker and draw fangs on the next mask off the press, and she laughs, startled, and draws fangs on the one after that herself.
success.art: A blond girl and a teenager laughing together beside a mask press in a green-lit garage, both drawing little vampire fangs on smiling paper masks with markers, a tiny pair of fangs inked on the girl's hand

failure.text: "Anything?" Kimmy repeats, and the hum rises around her. "We would be what everyone is." She rubs the fangs off her hand with her thumb until the skin is pink, and goes back to feeding the press.
failure.art: A tired blond girl rubbing ink off the back of her hand beside a thumping mask press, green light humming around her, a teenager watching sadly from beneath the half-open garage door

choices.label: Sneak around back and let the air out of the delivery van's tires

success.text: Behind the garage a beige delivery van sits loaded with mask boxes for the morning. Hiss, hiss, hiss, hiss. By the time Rex Brightwater comes out jingling the keys, the van is sitting on its rims. He stares at the flat tires for a long time, unable to decide what a normal person does next.
success.art: A blond man in khakis staring blankly at a beige delivery van sitting on four flat tires behind a suburban garage at night, cardboard boxes stacked inside, a teenager hiding behind a trash can

failure.text: The valve cap sticks, and while you wrestle with it, a car door opens. Rex Brightwater is sitting in the driver's seat, smiling, as if he has been sitting there all night. "Need a ride somewhere, champ?"
failure.art: A smiling blond man in khakis leaning out of the driver's door of a beige delivery van at night, a startled teenager crouched by the rear tire, green light glowing from the garage

finale.title: Isn't It a Beautiful Day
finale.text: The Halloween parade on Crystal Street is perfect. Everyone wears the same costume: a smiling paper Brightwater mask. The pods in the basement of 7 are opening one by one. Rex and Donna stand on the roundabout as their faces split down the middle like seeds, and green light pours out, and the hive speaks in every neighbor's voice at once: "We heard you. You asked for everyone the same. Why are you fighting the thing you wished for?"
finale.art: A suburban Halloween parade on a cul-de-sac at night where every marcher wears the same smiling paper face mask, on the roundabout beside a purple crystal rock a blond couple in pastel sweaters whose faces are splitting open down the middle with green light pouring out, open green pods glowing in a basement window nearby, four teenagers in loud mismatched costumes facing them, green and violet light, wide shot

choices.label: Storm the basement and rip the pods open by hand

success.text: You tear through the basement pod by pod and drag your neighbors out, wet and gasping and themselves. Upstairs, the copies wilt like cut flowers. The Brightwaters fold into the lawn and are gone by morning, leaving four perfect circles of dead grass.
success.art: A teen ripping open a glowing green pod in a dark basement as a gasping goth teen tumbles out, wilted pastel copies collapsing upstairs

failure.text: There are too many pods, and every one you open closes again. A hundred paper masks turn toward you. The hum fills your skull until you almost say it with them.
failure.art: Rows of resealing green pods in a basement and a hundred paper-masked neighbors on the stairs turning toward a struggling teen

choices.label: Hijack the parade PA and blast the loudest, strangest song you own

success.text: Feedback, then a synth scream, then the weirdest B-side on your mixtape at full volume. The hum shatters. Masks fall off, and the copies drop where they stand like puppets with cut strings. The hive flees back up into the sky, offended by your taste in music.
success.art: A teen at a parade sound booth cranking a cassette deck to full volume, paper masks flying off marchers, a streak of green light retreating into the night sky

failure.text: The PA plays the hum instead of your tape, a thousand times louder. The parade turns its masks toward the booth and begins, very politely, to walk toward you.
failure.art: A parade of paper-masked marchers turning in unison toward a sound booth, speakers glowing green, a teen ejecting a useless cassette

choices.label: Gather the town's weirdos and make everyone say out loud what they love about them

success.text: Glory takes the mic. Raven, Vernon's Caverns and Chimeras group and the Glitter Box chorus line climb up beside you. You read the old letters, and then you read the names. "Vernon Kessler, who taught half of us to play Caverns and Chimeras. Shelby Duarte, who made the best Halloween makeup in town." Neighbors start shouting their own: the accordion man, the girl in the cape. With every name said with love, a pod opens. The hive goes quiet. It finally understands what the town really wanted.
success.art: A drag queen with a microphone, goth teens, nerds and chorus dancers on a roundabout beside a teen reading names aloud, green pods opening behind them, neighbors pulling off paper masks and cheering

failure.text: Your voice is lost under the hum. A few neighbors lift their masks, then lower them again, unsure. They are not ready to be loud yet. You need them to hear the whole truth.
failure.art: A teen shouting into a microphone while a few paper-masked neighbors half-lift their masks and hesitate, green light rising around them

choices.label: Hit the hum with the weirdest truths you know, the kind that glitched it that first week

success.text: That first week taught you the hive's blind spot: it can copy anything but weird. So you climb the roundabout and shout the strangest true things you know. "I eat cereal with orange juice! Mr. Okafor talks to his tomatoes! Raven held a funeral for a mushroom!" Behind the paper masks the neighbors start shouting their own, far too strange to copy, and the hum skips like a scratched record; the masks crumple, the copies freeze mid-step, and the hive, unable to make the town match, pulls its green light back into the sky like a tide going out.
success.art: A costumed teenager shouting joyfully from atop a glowing purple geode on a suburban roundabout, neighbors tearing off crumpled paper masks and laughing, green light streaming back up into the night sky

failure.text: Your weirdest truth comes out sounding perfectly normal, and the hum swallows it. A hundred paper masks tilt toward you, interested. "We like that too," they say together, and your skin crawls.
failure.art: A crowd of neighbors in identical smiling paper masks tilting their heads toward a costumed teenager on a roundabout at night, green light pouring up from the roundabout behind them

choices.label: Climb the roundabout and refuse out loud, the way you stood up in public midweek

success.text: Midweek you learned that the hive hates one thing even more than a mess: somebody refusing in public, where real people can see. So you climb the roundabout and shout it over the hum. "NO! We didn't wish for this! We take it back!" The neighbors who watched you stand out this week tear off their paper masks and shout it with you, and your crew storms the basement of number 7, ripping pods open while the copies wilt like cut flowers. By midnight the Brightwaters have folded into their lawn, and Crystal Street is loud again.
success.art: A costumed teenager standing defiantly on a glowing geode shouting, neighbors ripping off paper masks and raising fists, teenagers hauling neighbors out of green pods through a basement window, a parade scattered across the street

failure.text: You shout, and the hum answers in a hundred voices, sweet and patient. A few neighbors lift their masks, then lower them again. They heard you, though, and some of them keep their hands close to their faces.
failure.art: A costumed teenager shouting from a roundabout at a crowd in smiling paper masks, a few neighbors lifting their masks halfway with uncertain eyes, green light humming over the street

choices.label: Name what makes each neighbor strange and wonderful, like the night before Halloween taught you

success.text: The night before Halloween proved it: under every copy is somebody specific, somebody no pod could hold. So you walk the parade and say it to each mask. "Vernon, who taught half of us Caverns and Chimeras. Shelby, who does the best Halloween makeup in town." Masks start coming off, the neighbors start shouting the weird, wonderful things they love about each other, and with every name a pod in the basement opens, until the hive goes quiet and finally understands what the town really wanted: not everyone the same, only nobody alone.
success.art: A joyful Halloween parade on a suburban street, neighbors pulling off paper masks and hugging, a blond girl lowering her own paper mask in wonder, green light softening into dawn

failure.text: You call out the first name, and the hum drowns the rest. The masks turn toward you, curious and patient. You know exactly what to say, but the street is not brave enough yet to say it with you.
failure.art: A costumed teenager calling out into a parade of neighbors in identical smiling paper masks, the masked faces turning slowly toward them, green light pulsing from a basement window

best.title: The Weirdo Parade
best.text: On November first Glimmer Falls holds its first annual Weirdo Parade. The Glitter Box leads in sequins, the goths march in velvet, the AV club rolls a cardboard starship down Main Street, Vernon wears his space-captain uniform and Shelby does everyone's makeup. The PTA petition is shredded and thrown as confetti. And one Brightwater, Kip, does not go home with the hive. He dyes his hair green, joins the yearbook club, and takes the worst, blurriest, most wonderful photos anyone has ever seen.
best.art: A joyful small-town parade on Main Street in daylight, drag performers in sequins leading, goth teens in velvet, kids pushing a cardboard starship, a boy in a homemade space-captain uniform, shredded paper confetti in the air, and a blond teenage boy with freshly dyed green hair snapping a photo with a 35mm camera, bright autumn sun, wide shot

good.title: For Sale: 7 Crystal Street
good.text: The pods are gone, the copies are gone, and the neighbors who vanished come home a little confused and very hungry. The Brightwaters' house goes back on the market. But the petition to close the Glitter Box is still circulating at church, and nobody ever really asks why the hive found such an easy home here.
good.art: An empty pastel split-level house behind a realtor stake on a dead brown lawn, a clipboard of paper left on the porch rail, a teenager on the sidewalk staring at it with hands in their jacket pockets, gray November afternoon light, wide shot

bittersweet.title: A Little Too Nice
bittersweet.text: Everyone comes back from the basement. Almost all the way. Vernon never puts his uniform on again, and Shelby keeps her lipstick in a drawer. They say they just grew out of it. You catch them sometimes, staring at nothing and humming, and you have to say their names twice before they look up.
bittersweet.art: A teenager in a plain buttoned collared shirt sitting at a school desk and staring out a classroom window, humming, beside them an open desk drawer holding a tube of black lipstick and a small rocket-ship pin, flat afternoon light through the glass, medium shot

bad.title: Isn't It a Beautiful Day
bad.text: On November first you wake up in a mint cardigan and you feel wonderful. You wave to the Brightwaters across the street. You agree with everyone. When your crew bangs on your door shouting your name, you smile at them kindly, because they look so tired from being different, and you hope they come to dinner soon.
bad.art: A teenager in a mint cardigan smiling serenely and waving from a perfect green lawn, three worried friends in mismatched jackets shouting from the sidewalk, and across the street a smiling blond family in pastel sweaters waving back, bright flat morning sun, wide shot
